newsitem.title: GERMANY: Days seen numbered for German "wage cartels".
newsitem.headline: Days seen numbered for German "wage cartels".

text.p: German industry's divided reaction to implementing cuts to sick-pay benefits could signal the beginning of the end for Germany's once-powerful "wage cartels", economists and analysts said on Wednesday.

The decision by firms such as carmakers BMW AG and Volkswagen AG's Audi unit not to follow behind Daimler-Benz AG in putting the cuts into action defies the advice given by the industry association Gesamtmetall.
This undermining of collective bargaining is seen as the main consequence of moves by carmakers in the last few days to go their own ways in handling huge worker resistence to the cut in benefits.
"Particularly after unification, there has been a growing feeling that the wage cartels have served the economy badly," said Thomas Mayer, senior economist at Goldman Sachs in Frankfurt.

Mayer said industry associations such as Gesamtmetall had, along with the trade unions, created a de facto cartel that was now proving ineffective in regulating labour markets flooded with an oversupply of workers in former Communist East Germany.
Unemployment -- currently riding at a post-war high of some four million -- has been the result of a tendency in the past to set collective wage agreements too high, Mayer said.
In particular, he criticised last year's four percent wage rise in the metal and engineering sector as "disastrous" for German labour markets.

While the decision by Audi and BMW not to implement the new law, which would allow them to cut sick pay entitlements by 20 percent, ostensibly means they are stuck with higher costs, few economists doubt they too would follow Daimler at a later date.

BMW's decision to maintain full sick pay entitlements in what it has called "the interest of internal industrial peace" is widely seen as part of a less hard-line strategy to find a way of introducing the cuts in future wage agreements.
"I don't think that long-term there is any doubt that these companies will put through the cuts too," said one economist who asked not to be named.

But some economists, while accepting that the move towards individual companies negotiating their own wage deals was likely to continue, said the demise of collective bargaining could have some disadvantages for German industry.

"In the past we have seen that collective wage agreements for a sector have forced the least productive firms in that sector to improve their productivity," Herman Remsperger, chief economist at BHF Bank in Frankfurt, said.
But he added that Germany's famous system of "social consensus", of which agreement between employers and workers formed a key part, was less suited when the issue was a reduction in labour costs.

"Consensus has been fine in the past when it's been about rises in wage deals. But this is really the first time that it's been about making cuts and the current system doesn't appear to work for that," Remsperger said.
